title: Maximum Likelihood & ANOVA
subtitle: Contact session 10 · slides CS-10 · MLE, F-test, one-way and two-way ANOVA

lesson.title: Why this matters in AI and ML
lesson.lead: MLE trains models. ANOVA and the F-test tell you whether a difference is real or just noise.

blocks.text: Maximum likelihood = how models learn

When you train a classifier with cross-entropy loss, you are doing maximum likelihood: you pick the weights that make the training data most likely. Logistic regression, naive Bayes and the Gaussian fits inside a GMM all work this way. Today you meet the idea in its smallest form: one unknown number (a probability, a mean) and some data.
ANOVA and the F-test = is the difference real?

items: **Comparing models:** three models each scored on five test folds. Are their average scores really different, or is it fold-to-fold noise? That is one-way ANOVA.
**Comparing models and datasets together:** models are the treatments and datasets are the blocks. That is two-way ANOVA.
**Comparing spreads:** is model A's error more variable than model B's? That is the F-test for two variances.

blocks.label: Big picture
blocks.text: The slides use MLE and ANOVA on small hand-sized data. The thinking is identical to the ML version: assume a distribution, estimate a number, then ask whether a difference is bigger than noise.

lesson.title: MLE: the idea (slides 3–12)
lesson.lead: Flip the question: instead of asking how likely the data is for a known θ, find the θ that makes the data most likely.

blocks.text: Probability asks: *given θ, how likely is this data?* Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) asks the reverse: *given this data, which θ makes it most likely?* The function being maximised is the **likelihood** L(θ), the joint probability of the sample read as a function of θ.
L(θ) = f(x₁|θ) · f(x₂|θ) · … · f(xₙ|θ) = ∏ f(xᵢ|θ)
blocks.caption: Independent observations, so the probabilities multiply.

blocks.text: The helmet example from class (slides 7–12)
Ten helmets are tested. The 1st, 3rd and 10th are flawed (X = 1), the other seven are fine (X = 0). Each X has pmf p^x (1 − p)^(1−x), so the joint probability is:
f(x₁,…,x₁₀; p) = p³ (1 − p)⁷
The graph of L(p) peaks just above 0.3. Calculus finds the exact peak. Take the natural log first, because a sum is easier to differentiate than a product:

blocks.label: Teacher says
blocks.text: If you are only told *3 of 10* were flawed, you get the same estimate p̂ = 3/10. The order does not matter (slide 12).

lesson.title: The MLE recipe and the three results
lesson.lead: Five steps every time. You only need to remember the three answers.

blocks.text: The 5-step recipe (slides 13–15)

items: Write the likelihood: **L(θ) = ∏ f(xᵢ | θ)**.
Take the log: **ℓ(θ) = ln L(θ)**. Products become sums.
Differentiate with respect to θ.
Set the derivative **equal to 0**.
Solve for θ. The solution is **θ̂**, the maximum likelihood estimate.

blocks.text: The three results you need (slides 16–20)

head: Distribution
Likelihood ingredient
MLE
rows: L = e^(−nμ) μ^(nX̄), ℓ = −nμ + nX̄ ln μ

blocks.text: Symbols: n = sample size, k = number of successes, X̄ = sample mean, Xᵢ = each observation.

blocks.label: Exam trap
blocks.text: The Normal MLE of the variance divides by **n**, not n − 1. The professor pointed out that the unbiased estimate uses 1/(n − 1). The MLE is the biased one. Use n when the question says MLE.

blocks.label: Teacher says
blocks.text: You do not need to memorise ln f for the Normal. Know the recipe and the three results. The slides omit the Normal derivation.

lesson.title: Using the MLE: how it is asked
lesson.lead: Estimate first, then plug the estimate into a probability. This is the invariance property.

blocks.text: The MLE of a *function* of the parameter is that function of the MLE. So after you find μ̂ or θ̂, write "by invariance, replace the parameter by its MLE" and use the usual probability formula. (This idea is in the textbook; write it as a one-line reason in the exam.)

head: They ask
Use
Source
rows: scale μ̂ first (2 calls → 2μ̂), then use the formula
Binomial: exactly k out of n

blocks.label: Why the shortcut works
blocks.text: θ̂ᵏ is just the full binomial formula with n = k: C(k,k) = 1 and (1 − θ̂)⁰ = 1.

blocks.label: Common mistake
blocks.text: e^(−2.6) is a **positive** number (= 1/e^2.6 = 0.0743). The minus sign belongs to the exponent only, so (1 + μ) e^(−μ) is never negative. A probability is always between 0 and 1.

blocks.label: Common mistake
blocks.text: Poisson window: if μ̂ is per call and they ask about the next 2 calls, use μ = 2 × μ̂. Do not reuse μ̂ as it is.
How it appeared in the 2024 end-sem (4 marks)

"Accidents per day follow a Poisson distribution. Over five days the counts were 4, 2, 5, 3 and 6. (i) Find the MLE of the average accidents per day. (ii) Using it, estimate the probability of no accidents on a day." The answer is μ̂ = 4 and P(0) = e⁻⁴ = 0.0183.

lesson.title: F-test for two variances (slides 21–23)
lesson.lead: One ratio of two sample variances. Not the same thing as ANOVA, although both use the F table.

blocks.text: Use this when the question asks whether one process is **more variable** than another, or whether two variances are equal. There are two samples and one ratio.
F = s₁² / s₂²   with the larger variance on top,   df = (n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1)
Standard steps

items: State H₀: σ₁² = σ₂² and H₁ (σ₁² > σ₂², or ≠).
Write α.
Compute F = larger s² ÷ smaller s². If the question gives the **standard deviation**, square it first. If it gives the **variance**, do not square again.
df = (n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1): numerator sample first.
Look up F in the table at α (see the F-table board).
If F > the table value, reject H₀. Otherwise do not reject.

blocks.label: Exam trap
blocks.text: **Direction check.** For H₁: σ₁² > σ₂², the sample variance of group 1 must really be the larger one. If it is smaller, F is below 1 on the wrong side, so do not reject before computing anything.

blocks.label: Exam trap
blocks.text: Two-tailed F-test uses **α/2** on the upper tail. The exam F-table prints only α = 0.05, so a 0.025 table is not available. Expect one-tailed questions.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: The larger variance goes on top so F is always at least 1. That is why we only look at the upper tail.

lesson.title: One-way ANOVA: the idea and the formulas (slides 24–29)
lesson.lead: Compare three or more means by comparing two kinds of variance.

blocks.text: With k groups you could run many two-sample tests, but errors pile up. ANOVA tests **all the means at once**: H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = … = μₖ against H₁: not all equal.
The idea

items: **Between-group variation (SSTR):** how far the group means sit from the overall mean.
**Within-group variation (SSE):** how spread out the values are inside each group. This is the noise.
If the between-group part is large compared with the noise, the means really differ.

blocks.text: Formulas in the slide notation
Symbols: k = number of groups, nⱼ = size of group j, n = total observations, x̄ⱼ = mean of group j, x̄ = overall mean, r = group size (when equal).
The F test is **right-tailed**: reject H₀ if F is bigger than the table value.

blocks.label: Assumptions
blocks.text: Slide 25 lists three assumptions: each population is normal, the variances are equal, and the samples are independent.

blocks.label: Wording
blocks.text: The slides say "accept H₀" when F is not big enough. You can write "do not reject". If your answer sheet follows the slides, "accept" is fine.

lesson.title: One-way ANOVA: the shortcut (CF) method step by step
lesson.lead: Method-2 in your slides. Same answer as Method-1, with far less arithmetic.

blocks.text: Symbols
k = number of groups, nⱼ = size of group j, n = total, Cⱼ = total of group j, G = grand total.
The steps (slides 33–34 and 53)

items: **H₀ and H₁.** H₀: all means equal. State α.
**Group totals Cⱼ and grand total G.**
**CF = G² / n.** The "nothing is different" baseline.
**SST = ΣΣx² − CF.** Square every single value, add, subtract CF.
**SSTR = Σ(Cⱼ² / nⱼ) − CF.** Square each group *total*, divide by that group's size.
**SSE = SST − SSTR.**
**df and MS:** MSTR = SSTR/(k − 1), MSE = SSE/(n − k).
**F = MSTR / MSE.**
**Table value** at (k − 1, n − k). If F > table, reject H₀.
**Conclusion in a sentence.**

blocks.text: Slide 30 example, both methods

blocks.label: Exam trap
blocks.text: Step 4 squares **individual values**. Step 5 squares **group totals**. Mixing the two is the most common slip.

lesson.title: How to read the F-table
lesson.lead: Two numbers pick the cell: DF1 across the top, DF2 down the side.

blocks.text: The exam paper prints the F table for **α = 0.05** only (the slides show the same page, PDF page 516). Each cell is the table value F(DF1, DF2).

head: Meaning
Goes
rows: df of the thing on **top** of F (numerator)
df of the thing on the **bottom** of F (always MSE)

blocks.text: What DF1 and DF2 are in each test

blocks.label: Exam trap
blocks.text: The table rows jump 30 → 40 → 60 → 120 → ∞. If your DF2 is not printed (say 36), use the **nearest row** that is printed, here 40. Never invent a cell.

blocks.label: Careful
blocks.text: One table per α. The slides compare with the 5% value unless told otherwise. One slide example (iron intake, slide 35) uses the 1% value by mistake. See the slide-quirks board.

lesson.title: Two-way ANOVA: steps, formulas and both dfs (slides 37–48)
lesson.lead: Two factors at once: the Treatment you compare and the Block you control for.

blocks.text: The grouping factor is the **Treatment** (columns). The control factor is the **Block** (rows). Adding the block takes variation out of the error, so the test is more sensitive (slide 37).
Symbols (slide 40)
k = number of treatments (columns), m = number of blocks (rows), n = k · m, G = grand total.
Formulas
Standard steps

items: **Two pairs of hypotheses** (slide 38): H₀₁ for treatments, H₀₂ for blocks. Write α.
**Table with row totals, column totals and G.**
**CF = G²/n.**
**SST = ΣΣx² − CF.**
**SSTR** from the column totals, divisor m.
**SSBL** from the row totals, divisor k.
**SSE = SST − SSTR − SSBL.**
**df and mean squares** for treatments, blocks and error.
**Two F values**, both over the same MSE.
**Two table values** (DF1 differs, DF2 is the same). Compare each separately.
**Conclusion for each factor** in plain English.

blocks.text: One-way versus two-way

blocks.label: Exam trap
blocks.text: Swapping k and m. Column totals are divided by m (the number of values in a column). Row totals are divided by k. Check: SSTR + SSBL + SSE = SST, and the three df add up to n − 1.

blocks.label: Exam trap
blocks.text: Using one table value for both F tests. DF1 is different for the two factors, so look up two values.

blocks.text: Last-minute checklist

items: MLE: μ̂ = X̄, θ̂ = k/n, σ̂² divides by n. Then plug in.
F-test: larger on top, df = (n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1), check direction.
One-way: CF, SST, SSTR, SSE, F = MSTR/MSE, df (k − 1, n − k).
Two-way: add SSBL, df (k − 1)(m − 1), two F values, two lookups.
Always write the conclusion in words.

problem.text: The number of defective hard drives produced daily follows a Poisson distribution. The counts for ten days are 7, 3, 1, 2, 4, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2. Find the maximum likelihood estimate of the probability of 0 or 1 defectives on one day.

steps.label: Model
steps.text: X ~ Poisson(μ), with P(X = x) = e^(−μ) μ^x / x!

steps.label: Estimator
steps.text: The MLE of the Poisson mean is μ̂ = X̄ (slides 17–18).

steps.label: Sentence
steps.text: The estimated probability of at most one defective on a day is about 0.267.

problem.text: Car accidents per day follow a Poisson distribution. On five days the counts were 4, 2, 5, 3 and 6. (i) Find the MLE of the average number of accidents per day. (ii) Using it, estimate the probability of no accidents on a day. [4 marks]
Ten helmets are tested. The 1st, 3rd and 10th are flawed. Find the MLE of p, the probability that a helmet is flawed.

steps.label: Model
steps.text: Each Xᵢ is Bernoulli(p): Xᵢ = 1 if flawed, 0 if not. Three are 1, seven are 0.

steps.label: Log
steps.text: ln L = 3 ln p + 7 ln(1 − p).

steps.label: Solve
steps.text: p̂ = **3/10 = 0.3**. It is the sample proportion, k/n.

problem.text: A server's disconnects per day over 5 days were 3, 5, 4, 6, 2. Estimate the probability of at least 3 disconnects on a day.

steps.label: Terms
steps.text: P(0) = e⁻⁴, P(1) = 4e⁻⁴, P(2) = 8e⁻⁴. The sum is 13e⁻⁴.

problem.text: Dropped connections in 4 calls were 3, 0, 2, 1. Find the probability that the next two calls have no drops at all.

steps.label: Window
steps.text: Two calls, so the mean for two calls is 2 × 1.5 = **3**.

problem.text: In a test, 48 of 60 transceivers pass. Estimate the probability that the next two both pass.
In a test, 98 of 100 insulators survive. Estimate the probability that three insulators in a row survive.

worked.title: MLE · Chips: next two, and exactly six

problem.text: In a batch of 40 chips, 6 are defective. (a) Find the MLE of the defect probability. (b) Probability that the next two chips are both defective. (c) Probability that exactly 6 of the next 10 are defective.

steps.label: (b)
steps.text: Both of the next two: θ̂² = 0.15² = **0.0225**.

steps.label: (c) Formula
steps.text: Exactly k of n: C(n,k) θ̂ᵏ (1 − θ̂)ⁿ⁻ᵏ with n = 10, k = 6.

steps.label: Note
steps.text: (b) is the full formula with n = k = 2. The C(n,k) factor counts the ways the 6 defectives can sit among 10 chips.

problem.text: A sample from a Normal distribution is 2, 5, 8, 9. Find the MLE of μ and σ².

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: The unbiased sample variance would be 30/3 = 10. The MLE is the 7.5.

problem.text: Method A: 10 shafts, s = 0.032 mm. Method B: 14 shafts, s = 0.028 mm. At 5%, is there evidence that Method A has greater variability than Method B? [4 marks]

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: H₀: σ_A² = σ_B². H₁: σ_A² > σ_B² (right-tailed). α = 0.05.

steps.label: Direction
steps.text: A's variance is the larger one, so it goes on top and the direction is right.

steps.label: Sentence
steps.text: At 5% there is not enough evidence that Method A is more variable than Method B.

problem.text: Sample 1: n₁ = 9, s₁² = 4. Sample 2: n₂ = 13, s₂² = 9. At 5%, test H₁: σ₁² > σ₂².

steps.label: Direction check
steps.text: H₁ says σ₁² is the bigger one, but the sample variance of group 1 (4) is smaller than group 2 (9).

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.text: The data point the other way, so there is no evidence for H₁. **Do not reject H₀** without any further calculation.

steps.label: If it were two-tailed
steps.text: F = 9/4 = 2.25 with df (12, 8), compared with the upper α/2 value.

problem.text: Test at 5% whether the means of three samples from normal populations with equal variances differ. G1: 8, 10, 7, 14, 11. G2: 7, 5, 10, 9, 9. G3: 12, 9, 13, 12, 14.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃. H₁: not all equal. α = 0.05. k = 3, n = 15.

steps.label: Decision
steps.text: 4.0 > 3.89, so **reject H₀**: at least one group mean differs.

problem.text: Test at 5% whether the mean iron intake differs among four groups of patients (n = 40). The slide gives SSTR = 349.52 and SSE = 922.95.

steps.label: Table
steps.text: F(0.05; 3, 36) is not printed. The nearest row, 40, gives **2.84** (the exact value is about 2.87). The slide compares with 4.38, which is the 1% value.

steps.label: Decision
steps.text: 4.544 > 2.84, so **reject H₀**. The slide reaches the same decision.

problem.text: Three drying formulas are tested. A: 13, 10, 8, 11, 8. B: 13, 11, 14, 14. C: 17, 14, 13, 10, 11, 12. Test at 5% whether the mean curing time differs.

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: H₀: μ_A = μ_B = μ_C. k = 3, n = 15, α = 0.05. Unequal group sizes are fine.

steps.label: Decision
steps.text: 3.08 < 3.885, so **do not reject H₀**. There is no significant difference in curing time. The slide gives p = 0.084.

worked.title: Two-way ANOVA · Fertilizers and plots (slides 42–44)

problem.text: Three fertilizers are used on four plots. Yields: Nitrogen 6, 4, 8, 6 · Potash 7, 6, 6, 9 · Phosphate 8, 5, 10, 9 (plots A, B, C, D). At 5%, does the yield differ by fertilizer or by plot?

steps.label: Hypotheses
steps.text: H₀₁: plots do not differ. H₀₂: fertilizers do not differ. Plots are the treatments (columns), k = 4. Fertilizers are the blocks (rows), m = 3. n = 12.

steps.label: df and MS
steps.text: Plots: df 3, MSTR = 6. Fertilizers: df 2, MSBL = 4. Error: df (3)(2) = 6, MSE = 1.67.

steps.label: Decisions
steps.text: 3.6 < 4.76 and 2.4 < 5.14, so do not reject either H₀.

steps.label: Sentence
steps.text: At 5%, the yield does not differ significantly by plot or by fertilizer.

worked.answer: Plots F = 3.6 < 4.76 and fertilizers F = 2.4 < 5.14: neither is significant

worked.title: Two-way ANOVA · Teaching method and study time (slides 45–48)

problem.text: Test scores are recorded for three teaching methods and two study-time levels, with 3 scores per cell. At 5%, test the effect of teaching method and of study time. (The slide first averages the 3 scores in each cell.)

steps.label: Set-up
steps.text: Cell averages: Traditional 65, 71 · Online 57.67, 67.33 · Hybrid 64, 72.33 (less than 2 h, more than 2 h). Treatments (teaching method, columns) k = 3. Blocks (study time, rows) m = 2. n = 6.

steps.label: df and MS
steps.text: Methods: df 2, MSTR = 20.79. Study time: df 1, MSBL = 95.92. Error: df (2)(1) = 2, MSE = 1.72.

steps.label: Decisions
steps.text: Methods: 12.08 < 19.00, do not reject. Study time: 55.77 > 18.51, **reject**.

steps.label: Sentence
steps.text: Study time has a significant effect on the score. The teaching method does not, at 5%.

worked.answer: Methods F = 12.08 < 19.00 (not significant). Study time F = 55.77 > 18.51 (significant).

flashcards.back: Maximum likelihood estimation: choose the parameter value that makes the observed data most likely.
The product of the densities or pmfs of the observations, read as a function of θ: L(θ) = ∏ f(xᵢ | θ).
Write L, take ln, differentiate, set to 0, solve for θ̂.
θ̂ = k / n, the sample proportion.
μ̂ = X̄, the sample mean.
μ̂ = X̄ and σ̂² = Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²/n.

flashcards.front: Normal MLE variance: divide by n or n − 1?
flashcards.back: By n. The unbiased estimate uses n − 1; the MLE does not.
The MLE of a function of θ is that function of θ̂. So plug μ̂ or θ̂ into the probability formula.

flashcards.front: Poisson μ̂ is per call. The question asks about 2 calls. What now?
flashcards.back: Scale: use 2μ̂.
No. It is 0.0743. A probability is never negative.

flashcards.front: Binomial: probability that exactly k of n succeed?
flashcards.back: C(n,k) θ̂ᵏ (1 − θ̂)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. When all n succeed, this is θ̂ⁿ.
F = s₁²/s₂² with the larger variance on top, df = (n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1).

flashcards.front: The question gives s². Do you square it?
flashcards.back: No. Square only when the question gives standard deviations.
H₀: all group means are equal, against H₁: at least one differs.
Treatments k − 1, error n − k, total n − 1. F table at (k − 1, n − k).
CF = G²/n, SST = ΣΣx² − CF, SSTR = ΣCⱼ²/nⱼ − CF, SSE = SST − SSTR.
Normal populations, equal variances, independent samples.
SSTR = Σ(column total)²/m − CF. SSBL = Σ(row total)²/k − CF.
SSE = SST − SSTR − SSBL. df: k − 1, m − 1, (k − 1)(m − 1).

flashcards.front: How do you read the F table?
flashcards.back: DF1 (the numerator df) across the top, DF2 (the denominator df) down the side. The exam prints α = 0.05 only.

flashcards.front: Two-way: what are the two (DF1, DF2) pairs?
flashcards.back: Treatments (k − 1, (k − 1)(m − 1)). Blocks (m − 1, (k − 1)(m − 1)).

flashcards.front: The F table has no row for DF2 = 36. What now?
flashcards.back: Use the nearest printed row (40).

flashcards.front: Why do we add blocks in two-way ANOVA?
flashcards.back: The block removes variation from the error, so the test for the treatment is more sensitive.

quiz.q: The MLE of the mean of a Poisson distribution is…
quiz.explain: For Poisson the MLE is μ̂ = X̄ (slides 17–18).

quiz.q: The MLE of a Normal variance divides by…
quiz.explain: σ̂² = Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)²/n. The n − 1 version is the unbiased estimator.

quiz.q: In 40 trials there are 6 successes. The MLE of θ is…
Why do we take the log of the likelihood?
options: A sum is easier to differentiate than a product
quiz.explain: The log turns the product into a sum and has the same maximiser.

quiz.q: Which is the correct formula for the next 2 trials both succeeding?
quiz.explain: Independent trials multiply: θ̂ × θ̂.

quiz.q: μ̂ = 1.5 per call. The probability of no drops in the next 2 calls is…
quiz.explain: Scale to 2 calls: μ = 3, P(0) = e⁻³.

quiz.q: Is −3.6 e^(−2.6) a valid probability?
options: No, a probability can't be negative
quiz.explain: e^(−x) is positive, and so is (1 + μ) e^(−μ).

quiz.q: Poisson counts 3, 5, 4, 6, 2. Find μ̂.
With μ̂ = 4, find P(X = 0) = e⁻⁴.
9 of 25 pass. Find θ̂.
Normal data 2, 5, 8, 9. Find the MLE σ̂².
quiz.explain: Sum of squared deviations 30, divided by n = 4, gives 7.5.

quiz.q: In the F-test for two variances, the larger variance goes…
quiz.explain: The larger variance goes on top, so F ≥ 1.

quiz.q: df for the F-test with n₁ = 10 and n₂ = 14 is…
s₁ = 0.032 (n = 10) and s₂ = 0.028 (n = 14). Find F = s₁²/s₂².
One-way ANOVA with k = 4 groups and n = 40. The F table uses…
G = 150 and n = 15. What is the correction factor CF?
In SSTR = Σ(Cⱼ²/nⱼ) − CF, Cⱼ is…
quiz.explain: Square the group total and divide by the group size.

quiz.q: SSE in one-way ANOVA equals…
quiz.explain: SST = SSTR + SSE, so SSE = SST − SSTR.

quiz.q: In two-way ANOVA, SSE equals…
quiz.explain: Both the treatment and the block effects are taken out.

families.label: F-test
families.title: F-test: are two variances different?
families.lead: A single ratio of sample variances, with the larger on top.

blocks.text: The intuition
If two processes are equally steady, their sample variances should be close, so the ratio is near 1. A ratio far above 1 says the top one is more variable.
F = s₁² / s₂²,  df = (n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1)

families.label: One-way ANOVA
families.title: One-way ANOVA: do three or more means differ?
families.lead: Compare the variation between the groups with the variation inside them.

blocks.text: The intuition
Imagine three classes taking the same test. If the class averages are far apart compared with how spread out each class is, the classes really differ. ANOVA measures exactly that ratio.
CF = G²/n → SST = ΣΣx² − CF → SSTR = ΣCⱼ²/nⱼ − CF → SSE = SST − SSTR → F = MSTR/MSE
blocks.caption: df = (k − 1, n − k)

families.label: Two-way ANOVA
families.title: Two-way ANOVA: two factors at once
families.lead: A treatment you compare and a block you control for.

blocks.text: The intuition
Test scores may depend on both the teaching method and the study time. Two-way ANOVA separates the effect of each, and the leftover is the error.
SSE = SST − SSTR − SSBL
blocks.caption: Two F values, both over the same MSE. Treatments: (k − 1, (k − 1)(m − 1)). Blocks: (m − 1, (k − 1)(m − 1)).
